tier_reason: First-party numbers from public benchmark code (tests/bench_2k.rs, which times mozjpeg-rs against C mozjpeg built by mozjpeg-sys in the same process), but the README table states no CPU model, rustc version or RUSTFLAGS ('release mode with AVX2/NEON' only), so it falls short of A.

corrections.workload: One synthetic 2048x2048 RGB image (gradient plus periodic noise, generated in tests/bench_2k.rs), quality 85, 4:2:0, sequential (non-progressive) JPEG, single-threaded, 3 warmups then 30 timed iterations per side; Rust vs C mozjpeg built from the vendored source in the mozjpeg-sys 2.2.3 crate. Two configs: no optimizations (TestEncoderConfig::baseline(), Huffman optimization off) and Huffman optimization + AC and DC trellis with deringing off on both sides.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo test --release --test bench_2k -- --nocapture; README says 'release mode with AVX2/NEON'; rustc version and RUSTFLAGS for the README numbers are not stated (crate MSRV 1.89; the separate Criterion Docker harness benchmark/Dockerfile.perf pins rust:1.92-bookworm and installs nasm for mozjpeg-sys). C mozjpeg is the vendored source compiled by mozjpeg-sys.
corrections.caveats: Pure-Rust reimplementation (port) of the mozjpeg encoder with #![forbid(unsafe_code)], not a binding: C mozjpeg is used only as a dev-dependency for parity tests and benchmarks and as an optional config feature. The speed win exists only with trellis quantization (197 ms vs 210 ms, 6%) on one synthetic image; without trellis it is 4.6x slower (42 ms vs 9 ms). The README labels that row 'Baseline (huffman opt)', but the current tests/bench_2k.rs times TestEncoderConfig::baseline(), which has Huffman optimization off. The Rust trellis is TrellisMode::Optimized by default (adaptive search limiting, standard-table rate estimation), a different search from C mozjpeg's trellis, so outputs are not byte-identical; bench_2k discards the outputs and reports no file sizes, and the 0.05-0.80% smaller-file claim comes from a separate CID22 run (examples/cid22_bench). The bit-exact TrellisMode::MozjpegExact is described as slower and is not what was timed. No CPU model, rustc version or flags for the README table. An older checked-in benchmark/benchmark_results.csv (Kodak, 24 images x 21 qualities, progressive + trellis + deringing, from examples/pareto_benchmark built by a rust:1.83 Dockerfile from the project's earlier 'mozjpeg-oxide' name) sums to 6,850 ms Rust vs 10,658 ms C (about 36% less time, derived from page data) but with Rust files 0.9-3.9% larger at Q75-95, so it predates the current parity claims and states no CPU. README says much of the code is AI-generated and not fully human-reviewed; a 2026-07-28 note documents a NEON DCT bug that inverted blocks on aarch64 (fixed). The author recommends the sibling crate zenjpeg (already listed) for new projects. Baseline is C mozjpeg, not libjpeg-turbo or libpng.

notes: Port, not a binding, so not a duplicate; C mozjpeg (mozilla/mozjpeg) itself is not listed and could be a lead as the trellis-quantization incumbent. Trellis speed comparison is like-for-like in settings (Q85, 4:2:0, AC+DC trellis, Huffman opt, no deringing on both sides) but not in algorithm or output bytes. Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause, 3 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-29.

tier_reason: First-party README table with ns/op and file sizes for five gallery images against Go's image/png at png.BestCompression, but no benchmark code exists in the repo (no Benchmark functions in any *_test.go) and no Go version or CPU is stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'approximately 50% faster' than the standard Go PNG encoder and smaller files. Per image (image/png at BestCompression vs nativewebp at BestCompression, ns/op): 42,945,049 vs 35,413,726 ('17% faster', 120 kb vs 95 kb); 98,509,399 vs 42,626,779 ('57% faster', 46 vs 35 kb); 178,205,535 vs 96,800,750 ('46% faster', 236 vs 190 kb); 29,088,555 vs 19,877,708 ('32% faster', 53 vs 39 kb); 63,423,995 vs 27,813,126 ('56% faster', 139 vs 119 kb). The README's 'X% faster' is percent less time: 1.21x-2.31x per image, 1.85x in total (412.2 ms vs 222.5 ms), with WebP output 80.5% of the PNG bytes in total (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go benchmark output (ns/op); Go toolchain, flags and benchmark source not published (go.mod declares go 1.22.2, golang.org/x/image v0.24.0).
corrections.caveats: Different work from the baseline: nativewebp writes lossless WebP (VP8L) and image/png writes PNG with DEFLATE level 9, so the speed and size gains compare two formats, not two encoders of one format; both are lossless and both use their maximum-compression setting (nativewebp.BestCompression = method 6, added 2026-05-10 together with the revised README numbers). README calls it 'a quick benchmark': five images from Google's WebP lossless-and-alpha gallery, no harness in the repo, no hardware or Go version. Not compared against libwebp (cwebp -lossless), the natural WebP incumbent, so it shows nothing about speed against libwebp. Encoder is lossless only; decoding wraps golang.org/x/image/webp.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly. Kept at C; the 'about 50%' headline is close to the derived total (46% less time) but per-image gains range from 17% to 57% less time. Metadata checked: MIT, 462 stars, 20 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-05-10.

tier_reason: Decode numbers (~80 ms vs ~360/320 ms for Pillow) are first-party README figures with no harness, hardware, thread count or library versions; the NVENC encode claim ('milliseconds' vs 'dozens of seconds', '200x') has no measured numbers and is directional only.

corrections.baseline: Pillow with pillow-avif-plugin (libavif) for decode; software AV1 encoders (libaom, rav1e, SVT-AV1) for encode
corrections.claimed_speedup: README decode table for a 5184x3456 AVIF to NumPy: nvavif_py.decode_file() ~80 ms (disk I/O + decode + YUV to RGB) vs Pillow (pillow-avif-plugin) ~360 ms, OpenCV cv2.imread ~280 ms, imageio + av ~400 ms; a second table gives Pillow 320 ms and '4x'; summary '3-4x faster than standard tools'. Encode: NVENC 'milliseconds per image' and '200x' vs software CPU 'dozens of seconds per image' (no measured numbers).
corrections.caveats: Not an nvImageCodec binding: src/lib.rs decodes on the CPU with FFmpeg's libdav1d decoder via ffmpeg-next (threads=0 uses all cores) plus a custom fixed-point, rayon-parallel YUV to RGB conversion, and encodes with FFmpeg's av1_nvenc (NVIDIA Ada/Blackwell hardware encoder) or rav1e 0.7 as CPU fallback. The decode speedup is therefore mostly dav1d (already listed) running multithreaded against Pillow's plugin; the README says the plugin uses libaom, but pillow-avif-plugin's wheel build enables dav1d, libaom, rav1e and SVT-AV1 in libavif, so which decoder Pillow ran is unverified. No hardware, CPU or GPU model, thread counts, library versions or benchmark script; the two README tables disagree (320 ms vs 360 ms). The NVENC encode comparison is GPU hardware vs CPU software at unmatched quality settings, with no numbers. Single 'init' commit, 0 stars, PyPI 0.1.0 only.

notes: Batch premise was wrong: no nvImageCodec anywhere (Cargo.toml: pyo3, ffmpeg-next 8.1, avif-serialize, rayon, rav1e). Decode path is a wrapper over libdav1d, so duplicate of https://github.com/videolan/dav1d; the NVENC encode path is FFmpeg's av1_nvenc wrapper with directional claims only. If the orchestrator keeps it instead, tier C with the caveats above. Metadata checked: MIT, 0 stars, 1 commit dated 2026-04-11.
